title: Why Xiaomi's royalty payments became a customs duty fight in India
subtitle: The government told the Supreme Court that Xiaomi India and Flex did not fully disclose royalty deals, in a case worth more than $150 million.
content_html:
Picture a phone made in India. Many of its parts still arrive by ship or plane, and the brand also pays foreign companies a small fee for the technology inside. On 17 November 2026, Reuters reported, in a story carried by The Economic Times, that the Indian government told the Supreme Court that Xiaomi India and its former contract manufacturer Flex did not fully disclose the royalty deals of Xiaomi until investigators stepped in.

The case could cost Xiaomi's India unit more than $150 million. This is a tax fight, not a crime story. The heart of the case is one simple question: when a company pays for technology, does that payment belong in the value of the parts it brings into India?

Who is fighting, and over what?

Xiaomi, the Chinese phone brand, holds about 12% of the smartphone market in India. Its Indian arm, Xiaomi Technology India, is based in Bengaluru.

For years, Xiaomi did not bring in most phone parts itself. Its contract manufacturers in India imported the parts out of China, paid customs duties and then put the phones together, Reuters reported in February.

Xiaomi also paid royalties of 2% to 5% to foreign firms like Qualcomm for using their technology in those parts. A royalty is a fee you pay to use someone else's invention. Think of a band that pays the songwriter a little every time it plays his song.

In November 2025, a customs tax tribunal in Chennai (a special court for tax fights) held Xiaomi India liable for extra customs duty on royalties paid to Qualcomm and to Beijing Xiaomi Mobile Software. The notices covered imports from 1 April 2017 to 30 June 2020.

How big is the bill?

The tribunal's ruling puts the unpaid duty at $72 million. Under Indian law, that demand could grow to more than $150 million with interest and penalties if Xiaomi India loses. For a sense of size, the same report says Xiaomi India's profit was only $31.7 million in FY24.

The demand began with an investigation by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI). Three notices in the case demanded Rs 653 crore in duty for the same April 2017 to June 2020 period.

What did the government say this time?

Xiaomi took the tribunal ruling to the Supreme Court in January. In a 21 September filing asking the court to dismiss that challenge, the government said Xiaomi "knew the licensing arrangements under which it made the royalty payments and failed to make the required complete disclosure."

The filing also said Xiaomi shared the licence agreements only after the investigation began. A separate 11 September filing said Flex was liable for "failing to place the underlying contractual structure before the customs authorities". Flex's Indian unit, Flextronics Technologies India, has told the court that the company did not help Xiaomi undervalue imports.

Xiaomi and the tax authorities did not answer Reuters' questions on the filing. The government also said its case does not treat all contract manufacturing as wrong.

Why would a royalty change the customs bill?

Customs duty is a tax on goods that enter India. It is worked out on the value of the goods. So a higher value means a higher duty.

Here is a made-up example. Say a phone part is worth Rs 1,000 and the duty rate is 10%. The duty is Rs 100. Now say a 5% royalty, Rs 50, is tied to that part. If the royalty counts, the value becomes Rs 1,050 and the duty becomes Rs 105. Small for one part. Huge across millions of phones.

Think of a samosa stall that buys samosas for Rs 10 each, and also pays the recipe owner Rs 1 for every samosa. If the town charges a fee on what each samosa costs, should that Rs 1 count? That is the fight here.

The tribunal said yes. It relied on section 14 of the Customs Act and rule 10(1)(c) of the Customs Valuation Rules, which add some royalties and licence fees to the value of imported goods. It found that Xiaomi India paying the licence fee was a must before the parts were supplied to the factories.

What is a contract manufacturer?

A contract manufacturer is a factory that makes products for another brand. The brand designs and sells. The factory builds. It is like a sweet shop that orders laddoos from a big kitchen and sells them in its own boxes.

This kind of work has drawn Foxconn, Jabil and Tata Electronics to grow in India. In this case, the notices named four contract manufacturers, including Flextronics Technologies India and Rising Star Mobile India.

Xiaomi's view is simple: the factories imported the parts, and the royalties are a separate deal that should not attract duty. The tribunal saw it the other way. It found that the real control sat with Xiaomi India, and that the factories' rights were "very restricted".

In its Supreme Court challenge, Xiaomi said the ruling shows "an implicit mistrust of the entire contract manufacturing industry." Bharat FIH, a unit of Foxconn and another former Xiaomi contract manufacturer, is also challenging the ruling.

What does this mean for importers and phone makers?

A win for the government could bring similar checks in pharmaceuticals, autos and manufacturing, experts told Reuters. Many firms in these fields work with contract manufacturers in the same way.

"The Supreme Court ruling will be widely significant as it will specify the powers of Indian customs," New Delhi tax lawyer Tarun Jain told Reuters in February.

For any business that imports, the lesson is plain. Customs looks at the full deal, not just the invoice. The tribunal said it is for the companies to declare the facts about the patents involved at the time of import. Under that view, royalty and licence deals linked to imported goods belong in the papers given to customs.

The Supreme Court has not decided yet. Tax lawyers told Reuters that global investors and companies are watching the case closely.
